summary_paragraph: A 54-year-old woman with a history of Crohn’s disease, short bowel syndrome, and multiple prior abdominal surgeries was admitted for nausea, vomiting, and right upper quadrant abdominal pain. Imaging showed no evidence of bowel obstruction or Crohn’s flare, and she was managed supportively with IV fluids, antibiotics, and pain control. She developed right upper extremity swelling related to a midline catheter, and ultrasound confirmed a right subclavian vein thrombosis. Due to her history of heparin-induced thrombocytopenia, she was treated with Fondaparinux, which resolved the swelling. Her abdominal pain was partially exacerbated by PTSD and anxiety, for which she received Valium with a planned taper. She gradually advanced to a regular diet and was discharged home in stable condition after 15 days, with instructions to complete a 7-day Valium taper, finish a course of antibiotics, and follow up with her outpatient providers.
